passage: The tyre swing hung from the big neem tree behind the panchayat school, and the bell for the end of lunch would ring soon. Anirban had waited through three turns, counting the pushes under his breath. When the girl before him jumped off, he stepped forward, but Jeevan slid past him and dropped into the tyre, grinning. Heat rushed up Anirban's neck. His fists closed. "That's mine!" he shouted, so loudly that two goats by the wall lifted their heads. Jeevan blinked. "I didn't see you." Anirban didn't believe a word. He was certain Jeevan had watched him waiting and cut in anyway, just to win. Then the bell began to ring.

qa.q: Where did the tyre swing hang?
qa.a: It hung from the big neem tree behind the panchayat school.

qa.q: What did Anirban feel sure of when Jeevan got on the swing?
qa.a: He felt angry and cheated, with heat rushing up his neck, because he was certain Jeevan had watched him waiting and cut in just to win.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Anirban right now, before the quarrel grows?
qa.a: He could take one breath and check the facts, saying "I was next, can I go after you?" instead of assuming Jeevan meant it.

qa.q: How might Jeevan see Anirban's shout?
qa.a: Jeevan looks surprised and says they didn't see Anirban, so the shout may feel like an attack out of nowhere and make Jeevan want to defend too.

grounding: Shows a child flushing with unfairness when a friend takes the swing, shouting too loudly and assuming it was deliberate.

passage: Rain had left puddles under the climbing frame, so only one swing in the little park behind the apartment blocks in Porto was dry. Gabriel had been saving that swing in his head all afternoon. He wiped the seat with his sleeve, turned to wave at his dad on the bench, and when he turned back, Nadia was sitting on it, feet already off the ground. Something hot flashed in his chest. "That's mine!" he yelled, much louder than he meant, and his dad looked up from his phone. Nadia dragged her shoes to stop. "You weren't on it." "I wiped it! You saw me!" Gabriel was sure she had waited for him to look away. His face burned, and he planted himself in front of the swing so she couldn't go higher.

qa.q: What had the rain left under the climbing frame?
qa.a: The rain had left puddles under the climbing frame, so only one swing was dry.

qa.q: What did Gabriel believe about why Nadia took the swing?
qa.a: He believed she had waited for him to look away on purpose; his burning face and blocking the swing show how unfair it felt.

qa.q: What could Gabriel's dad do now to stop this small spark from spreading?
qa.a: He could come over calmly, say that Gabriel wiped the seat and Nadia may not have known, and help them agree on turns before blaming starts.

qa.q: How might Nadia feel when Gabriel shouts and blocks the swing?
qa.a: Nadia may feel accused and startled, because from her side the swing was empty, so she is likely to start defending herself.

grounding: Shows a boy feeling a flash of unfairness over a swing, shouting louder than he means and assuming the friend acted on purpose.

The tyre swing hung from the neem tree behind the panchayat school, and at lunch it was the only thing anyone wanted. Chaitanya had waited through three turns, counting the pushes. When the bell was two minutes away, he stepped forward.
Swati slid in from the other side and grabbed the rope.
"That's mine!" Chaitanya shouted, so loud that the boys by the handpump looked up. His ears burned. She had seen him waiting, he was certain. She always found a way to be first.
Swati blinked. "I didn't see you," she said, still holding the rope.
Chaitanya didn't believe a word of it.

qa.q: Where did the tyre swing hang?
qa.a: It hung from the neem tree behind the panchayat school.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when Swati grabbed the rope?
qa.a: He felt a hot rush of unfairness and anger; his ears burned and he was certain she had pushed in on purpose.

qa.q: What small pause could help Chaitanya at this moment, before the quarrel grows?
qa.a: He could take one breath and ask whether she saw him waiting, instead of deciding she meant it; that question could stop the fight before blame starts.

qa.q: What might Swati be experiencing when Chaitanya shouts?
qa.a: She seems startled and confused, and may feel accused of something she did not mean to do.

grounding: A boy loses the last swing turn to a friend, feels a jolt of unfairness and shouts too loudly, already sure she did it deliberately.

passage:
Tuan had counted to a hundred under the slide at the park in Melbourne, because Yosef said, "After a hundred, it's yours." The sun was low and Tuan's mum was already waving from the bench with his scooter.
At ninety-eight, Yosef's little sister ran over, and Yosef lifted her onto the swing.
"Hey! That's MINE!" Tuan's voice cracked across the whole playground. A dog barked. His chest felt hot and tight.
"She's only little," Yosef said.
"You did that on purpose," Tuan said. "You knew I was nearly there."
Yosef's face went red too. Tuan's mum called his name again.

qa.q: What number did Tuan count to while he waited?
qa.a: He counted to a hundred, and Yosef's sister got the swing at ninety-eight.

qa.q: Why did Tuan think Yosef did it on purpose?
qa.a: He felt cheated and angry; he had kept his side of the deal and it was nearly his turn, so it seemed planned rather than an accident.

qa.q: What turning point is still open to Tuan here?
qa.a: He could say what he felt, like "I waited ages and I'm upset," and ask for one quick turn, instead of accusing Yosef of a plan.

qa.q: What might Yosef be experiencing now?
qa.a: He may feel caught between his little sister and his friend, and embarrassed at being shouted at in front of everyone.

grounding: A boy who has waited for a swing sees a friend give it to someone else, shouts that it is his and assumes the friend meant it.

The after-school club at the community centre had one swing in the yard, and a chart on the door said whose turn it was. Joseph had checked it at snack time: his name came next.
When the helper opened the door, Simran ran straight to the swing and sat down.
"That's mine!" Joseph's shout bounced off the walls. The younger kids at the craft table went quiet. He could feel his face heating up, and he was already sure of it: Simran had read the chart too. She just didn't care.
Simran pointed at the door. "It says me."
Joseph didn't look at the chart.

qa.q: What was on the door of the community centre?
qa.a: A chart that said whose turn it was on the swing.

qa.q: How can you tell Joseph felt wronged when Simran sat on the swing?
qa.a: His shout bounced off the walls and his face heated up; he felt angry and cheated, sure she had read the chart and ignored it.

qa.q: What could Joseph do right now to stop this from growing into a fight?
qa.a: He could walk over and read the chart with Simran or ask the helper, checking the facts before deciding she meant to take his turn.

qa.q: How might Simran see Joseph's shout?
qa.a: She may feel confused and a bit defensive, because she believes the chart says it is her turn.

grounding: At a club, a boy sees another child take the swing he expected, shouts that it is his, and assumes she did it on purpose without checking.
